newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's ousted leftists vow to revamp party.
newsitem.headline: Romania's ousted leftists vow to revamp party.

text.p: Romania's ex-president Ion Iliescu called on Friday for an all-out revamping of his leftist party, which lost its seven-year grip on power at elections last November.

"The truth is that we lost the elections and as a party we are at a crossroads," Iliescu told the first conference of the Party of Social Democracy (PDSR) since their defeat to centrists in general and presidential elections.

Hundreds of delegates elected the veteran leader as party president at Friday's watershed meeting, called to vote a new statute and leadership for the PDSR, which had governed Romania in one form or another since the 1989 fall of communism.

"We must pool our forces and see what we have to do in order to regain popular confidence and to come back to government," said Iliescu, a former communist who lost last November's run-off ballot to reformist Emil Constantinescu.

The PSDR would seek a new niche in Romanian politics, as a centre-left opposition party, shedding its old image as a party of "managers" smeared by corruption scandals, said Iliescu, who leads the PDSR group in parliament's upper Senate.

Romanians, suffering plunging living standards and soaring prices in a painful transition to a free market, voted to remove Iliescu's leftwingers from office, completing their rout at local elections in June.
Iliescu, 66, said the PDSR had paid the price of botched reforms and of allowing itself to be dragged into corruption scandals, calling for new blood to be injected into the party.
"The party was sanctioned by a negative vote, generated by popular discontent over the way in which it governed," he said.
The PDSR would form a "constructive opposition" to Romania's new ruling centrist coalition, which has pledged a mix of fast reforms and social protection measures.

President Emil Constantinescu's centrists hold an absolute majority in parliament, where they rely on support from their coalition partners -- former prime minister Petre Roman's Democrats and an ethnic Hungarian party.

"This is the beginning of changes inside the party," said former Foreign Minister Teodor Melescanu, one of several senior diplomats drafted into the PDSR ahead of last year's polls in a bid to shore up its sagging electoral fortunes.
"We will draft alternative policies for this period, as well as for the time when early elections will be necessary," said Melescanu, recently appointed PSDR spokesman.

Local political analysts say the PDSR should remake itself as a modern party, dropping some of the ex-communists around Iliescu -- a self-confessed convert to market reforms -- if it wants a chance to regain some of its lost popular support.
